DOOM was the first true FPS (I'd call Wolf3D proto-FPS), it pioneered and popularized multi-player gaming, it was the first PC game to become enough of a pop-culture phenomenon to garner news reports, be slipped into TV shows, inspire novels, and it definitely helped push the burgeoning PC industry into the mainstream. It was the first major PC game to openly embrace/exploit the modding community, and was one of the first engines to be made open source to encourage further development. Every FPS around today can trace it's lineage back to DOOM, as can every game that supports multi-player.

I've actually thought about this quite a bit over the years. As my original post suggested, I was already a gamer when DOOM dropped, and I was playing & programming my own shit much earlier than that. Pong, Pac Man, Tetris and Mario are not PC games--they're either arcade or console games. They're great for sure, but I wouldn't conflate arcade or console games (especially early generation console games) with PC gaming. Half-Life was a ground breaking game that introduced a full narrative and more robust NPCs, but Half-Life was built on id's Quake engine. It wasn't revolutionary technologically, but it did raise the bar as far as storytelling in games. That was it's main impact. In fact, Half-Life's popularity nearly coincided with the decline of PC gaming and the rise of consoles as the predominant gaming platform. GTA is a great AAA franchise, but I'm at a loss on how it could be construed as technologically leaping ahead of everything that had come before. It didn't create a new genre of games. Don't get me wrong--it's a great franchise and IS innovative...but could you say that any single GTA game has had the import of DOOM? You also mention Wolf3D, and that is a tough one. I was around when Wolf3D was released too, and I actively handed out copies on 3.5" disks to my friends and co-workers. Wolf3D got a decent amount of attention, but it was released right before PCs really became mainstream--more precisely, it was optimized to run on 386 systems running DOS 5. It was very much a proto-FPS; most of the elements are there, but not all. And it never had the wide pop culture impact. It says something that folks are still playing, modding, and creating content for DOOM I & 2, but almost nobody is for Wolf3D.

Again, let me emphasize that I'm not arguing that DOOM is the greatest game ever made. There are shit-tons of awesome games. My only point is that no other single game in PC gaming history comes close to having the impact on the industry that DOOM did. I believe that will change within the next 5-10 years, however. If VR gaming takes off (and there is every reason to believe it will), then I would expect that some title will catch fire and rival or best DOOM's impact. That's what I hope at least--I've only ever seen one instance where a game leapfrogged ahead of everything else anyone had ever seen--and it was glorious.

Half-Life was built on the Quake engine. Valve modified it, but it was a licensed engine. Which is something else I forgot to credit DOOM with--it was one of the first PC gaming engines to enter into licensing deals (id had licensed the Wolf3D engine for Blake Stone released 2 weeks prior to DOOM). Heretic and Hexen were two of the biggest titles to license DOOM; Ken Silverman's Build engine, however, soon became a more popular choice until id made the Quake engine available.

Counter Strike began life as a mod to Half Life back in 1999. I do not know for sure, but it might very well have been inspired (in concept) by an extremely popular DOOM II mod called Marine Doom that was released in 1996. For those of you not born back then, Marine DOOM was a really big deal in the scene and it added a lot of legitimacy to the notion that gaming could be more than just recreational--that it could be employed to teach skills/tactics applicable to the real world. Marine DOOM got a lot of coverage in the media. I don't know for sure that it influenced the development of Counter Strike since those devs also produced a Quake mod called "Navy Seals" in 1998, but I'd say there is an excellent chance it did.
